newsitem.title: IRAN: OPEC bid to plug output leaks seen failing.
newsitem.headline: OPEC bid to plug output leaks seen failing.

text.p: OPEC's latest attempt to stem runaway member country oil output looks doomed to failure, OPEC insiders and analysts said on Friday.

Seven Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) ministers, excluding linchpin Saudi Arabia, met in the ancient Persian city of Isfahan on Thursday and renewed pledges to stick to individual crude production allocations under OPEC's self-imposed but long-ignored ceiling.
The ministers warned that without plugging their leaky quota system sliding oil prices could fall further and put all too familiar pressures on national budgets.
They said there was a growing consensus among the group to keep its official 25.03 million barrels per day (bpd) ceiling unchanged when all 11 members meet in Vienna at the end of June.
Analysts said they saw no chance that OPEC's biggest quota busters, heavily represented in Isfahan by Venezuela and Nigeria, would stand by their renewed promise for collective restraint.
"I simply don't believe it," veteran OPEC watcher Mehdi Varzi of Kleinwort Benson told Reuters in Isfahan.
"I would be amazed if the likes of Venezuela reined back output. That would be very surprising."
"The days when Venezuela, Nigeria, Qatar and the like played a part in managing oil supplies as part of OPEC are gone," said an OPEC delegate.
"They have taken the commercial road, invited in foreign investment and raised capacity. They're not going to sit on that capacity and hand back market share to non-OPEC."
That leaves core Gulf OPEC members Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the UAE alone among world oil producers in keeping capacity in mothballs.
"There is a dynamic now for more and more OPEC producers to behave like non-OPEC producers," said Varzi.
Kuwaiti Oil Minister Isa Al-Mazeedi sent a veiled warning to those members violating quotas, suggesting Gulf OPEC patience was not endless.
"Self discipline is still exercised by a few key members but if this discipline is not maintained I don't dare speculate what prices will do," Mazeedi told an industry conference.
OPEC's second biggest producer Iran, struggling to attract much needed foreign investment to raise output capacity, led the rallying call on its own turf for renewed OPEC quota discipline.
"All of us feel we need to be careful about the market," said Iranian oil minister Gholamreza Aghazadeh. "Everybody agreed to follow his production quota."
"The level of OPEC oil had to be restrained and the countries have agreed to try and do this over the next few weeks," said OPEC Secretary-General Rilwanu Lukman.
Otherwise oil prices, down more than $6 at $18 a barrel this year for benchmark Brent, could fall further, said Lukman.
Actual OPEC output now is estimated running above 27 million barrels per day (bpd), two million bpd in excess of the official ceiling.
Individual quotas, with the exception of Iraq's, have not changed since September 1993.
Many observers think OPEC's oil Gulf guard is wasting its breath and pursuing outdated policies.
Former OPEC Secretary-General Subroto, speaking to Reuters earlier this week, said it was time the group dropped its ragged quota system and explicitly recognised revenues as its sole objective.
"I would suggest OPEC could work more smartly to optimise revenues," said Subroto. "In other words, not a strict quota policy."
Varzi said big Middle East OPEC producers need to open their oil industries to private investment or risk allowing massive oil reserves to lay fallow for some time to come.
"OPEC is addressing the new issues with oil policies," said Varzi.
"Do not rely on the market to bail you out. The way to compete with non-OPEC is to attract investment."
